clue.text: Forest spirit is winged beast

blocks.note: a greenwood is a forest in full leaf, the haunt of Robin Hood
in British slang your pecker is your courage, as in 'keep your pecker up'

explanation.surface: A woodland sprite turns out to be some kind of flying monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forest spirit' reads as one fairy-tale phrase, but splits into two words; 'keep your pecker up' is a British idiom meaning keep your spirits up.
explanation.definitionFit: The green woodpecker is a common European bird, so calling it a winged beast is a playful general description.

clue.text: Musician composed zero reggae

indicators.note: to compose is to put together and arrange, so the letters are set out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A musician has written a reggae track with nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the music theme so well that it hides its role as the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: George Ezra is an English singer-songwriter, known for hits like 'Budapest' and 'Shotgun'.

clue.text: Back in house, mature partygoer entertaining half-cut beer enthusiast

indicators.note: the back of a word is its tail end, so only its closing letter is wanted
cutting something in half throws away one of its two halves
a host entertaining a guest has them inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: the final letter of house
to mature is to age
a raver is someone who goes to raves or wild parties
the first half of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: At home, an older reveller is hosting a tipsy real-ale fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which suits the party, but here it trims the next word to half; that half then sits after the first letter of the partygoer.
explanation.definitionFit: An eager beaver is an idiom for a keen, overzealous person who throws themselves into every task.

clue.text: Made smart call circumventing a trap that’s set up

indicators.note: to circumvent is to go around, so one piece wraps around the rest
in a down clue, setting something up turns it to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: as in 'there's no call for that', meaning no need
taken as written
a net is a trap for fish or birds

explanation.surface: Someone tidied up a phone call that dodged a prepared ambush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call' looks like a phone call but means need, as in 'no call for it'; 'a' and the upturned trap sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To neaten is to tidy or smarten up, so the past tense describes something made smart.

clue.text: Rejects fast dismissed by talent scouts, unfortunately

indicators.note: something dismissed by a group is sent away from it, so those letters leave
an unfortunate outcome has gone wrong, so the remaining letters end up in a muddled order

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
taken as written

explanation.surface: Talent scouts sadly turn away hopefuls who are quick on their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like an adjective for speedy rejects, but it is the season of fasting, removed from the scouts before the rest is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Rejects as a noun means people cast aside by society, which is exactly what outcasts are.

clue.text: Boil green cabbage at start in school lesson

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
placing something in another puts it inside, between that word's letters

blocks.note: green in the environmental sense is eco
the opening letter of cabbage
DT is design and technology, a British school subject

explanation.surface: A cookery class begins by boiling green cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like a colour for the cabbage, but means environmentally friendly; DT (design and technology) is a subject in British schools.
explanation.definitionFit: To decoct is to extract the essence of something by boiling it down, a technical synonym for boil.

clue.text: Audio device connecting two parts of plant

blocks.note: the ear is the grain-bearing head of a cereal plant such as wheat
a bud is the unopened shoot or flower of a plant

explanation.surface: A gadget that plays sound is wired up to a pot plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The ear is the grain-bearing head of a cereal plant, and the bud is an unopened flower; the clue asks for both, joined.
explanation.definitionFit: An earbud is a tiny headphone worn inside the ear, a piece of equipment for listening to sound.

clue.text: Reportedly evasive fish

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: being coy is being evasive or reluctant to give details

explanation.surface: Word has it there is a shy fish about.
explanation.walkthrough: Coy means bashfully unwilling to commit, and it is pronounced exactly like the ornamental carp.
explanation.definitionFit: Koi are colourful ornamental carp, bred in Japan and kept in garden ponds.

clue.text: Way bar area fills

indicators.note: something that fills another occupies its interior, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: a rod is a metal bar
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: On the way, a pub's drinking area fills up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but it is a rod of metal; the single-letter area sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A road is a route for travel, and 'way' names such a route, as in 'the Appian Way'.

clue.text: Debauched toymaker with head back consuming wine

indicators.note: sending the head to the back moves the first letter round to the end
to consume is to take in, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: Corgi is a British maker of die-cast model cars
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine

explanation.surface: A dissolute toy manufacturer throws back his head while drinking wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toymaker' wants to be a person, but it is the brand Corgi, known for model cars; its first letter moves to the end before the wine goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Orgiastic describes wild, unrestrained revelry, the kind of behaviour called debauched.

clue.text: Fully shelled crab with a condiment

indicators.note: shelling removes the outer casing, and 'fully' means every word nearby loses its outside letters

blocks.note: the word with its outer letters removed
the word with its outer letters removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crab completely removed from its shell is served with a dipping sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word, but it is shelled too, alongside the crab; 'fully' extends the shelling to both words.
explanation.definitionFit: Raita is an Indian yoghurt side dish with cucumber or mint, served as a cooling accompaniment to curry.

clue.text: Plant seed endlessly? Billion times

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: germ is a seed, less its last letter
B is the abbreviation for billion
an era is a period of time, as in 'Victorian times'

explanation.surface: Sowing seed again and again, a billion times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a verb about sowing, but it is the noun being defined; 'times' is a period, not multiplication.
explanation.definitionFit: The gerbera is a daisy-like flowering plant from southern Africa, popular with florists.

clue.text: Got uneasy initially backing Mercury in Queen, perhaps

indicators.note: initially points to the start of a word, so only its first letter is kept
to back is to move backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction
being in something means sitting inside it, between its letters

blocks.note: the first letter of uneasy
Hg is the chemical symbol for mercury
a queen is a female cat; 'perhaps' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: A nervous fan backs Freddie Mercury of the band Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercury and Queen point to the rock band, but Mercury is the chemical element and a queen is a female cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Got and caught are interchangeable past tenses for seizing or contracting, as with a ball or a cold.

clue.text: Bed-wetter’s denial?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone insisting they did not wet the bed overnight
setter's reading: the gardener who waters flower beds is refused their usual watering tool during a drought

explanation.walkthrough: A bed here is a flower bed, and the bed-wetter is the gardener's watering kit; the denial is an official prohibition rather than an embarrassed child's protest.
explanation.definitionFit: Water companies in Britain impose this restriction in dry summers, forbidding garden watering with mains water.

clue.text: Contest is arranged to draw in right players

indicators.note: to arrange is to put in a new order, so the letters are reorganised
drawing something in takes it inside, so a letter is placed within the others

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A competition is set up to attract the right sort of athletes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests sport, alongside 'contest', but they are musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornetists play the cornet, a brass instrument, so they are players in the musical sense.

clue.text: Copper is one of those fellows accepted in European grants

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase rather than a synonym

indicators.note: being accepted in something means being taken inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
fellows are men
to grant permission is to let

explanation.surface: A police officer is one of the chaps admitted under EU funding schemes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' means a policeman on the surface, but here it is the metal; 'grants' is a verb, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is a chemical element, so the clue defines the answer by giving one example of the class.

clue.text: City where we see ladies or gents cycling

indicators.note: cycling sends letters round in a loop, so some move from the front to the back

blocks.note: the ladies and the gents are both public toilets, which the British call loos

explanation.surface: A town where men and women can be spotted riding bikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ladies or gents' looks like people, but means toilets, since loo is British slang for one; 'we' is a pun on wee.
explanation.definitionFit: Norway's capital is a plain example of the broad category, so the clue defines by naming its class.

clue.text: Fervour around mass campaign for computer program

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so the other pieces sit inside

blocks.note: fire is passion or fervour
M is the symbol for mass
a war can be a campaign against something, as in a war on drugs

explanation.surface: Zeal surrounds a mass campaign to get a new piece of software.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass campaign' reads as one phrase about a popular movement, but each word is its own piece, both housed inside the fervour.
explanation.definitionFit: Firmware is permanent software stored on hardware chips, a kind of program that runs a device.

clue.text: Revolutionary leader USA empowered — not totally deliberate

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the letters run backwards
not using the whole of the words means only a section of them is wanted

blocks.note: letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A rebel chief gave America only partial authority on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary leader' looks like a person such as Che or Mao, but 'revolutionary' just says to read the letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A measured response is careful and considered, the same sense as a deliberate one.

clue.text: Stray dog dropping tail

indicators.note: dropping the tail loses the final letter of the word

blocks.note: A traditional name for a dog

explanation.surface: A stray dog with its tail between its legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' is an adjective for the dog on the surface, but here it is a verb meaning to wander.
explanation.definitionFit: To rove is to wander about aimlessly, the same as straying.

clue.text: Uncertainty aboard the French vessel for vital period

indicators.note: being aboard means being on a ship, carried inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: an if is a doubt, as in 'no ifs or buts'
les is the plural French for 'the'
a pan is a cooking vessel

explanation.surface: Doubt aboard a French ship during a crucial stage of a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests the ship that 'aboard' sets up, but it is a cooking pan; the doubt goes inside the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifespan is the length of time something lives, so it is the period of being alive.

clue.text: Hunting beast exposed gruesome wound

indicators.note: exposing something strips off its covering, so the outer letters go
wound as in twisted round, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: the word with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: A predator reveals a horrible injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' reads as an injury but is the past of wind, meaning twisted.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouser is a cat valued for catching mice, so it is an animal that hunts.

clue.text: Journalist back on port becomes numb

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: ED is short for editor
Aden is a port city in Yemen

explanation.surface: A reporter returning to the harbour goes numb with cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Becomes numb' looks like the definition, but 'numb' is a verb here and 'becomes' only joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To numb something is to dull its feeling, which is what deadening does.

clue.text: Poet penning piece in centre of Canberra

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, as animals in a fold, so one item is held inside another
the centre of a word is its middle, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of the eight-letter word
a rook is a chess piece

explanation.surface: A poet in the middle of the Australian capital writes a piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' suggests a writer at work, but means enclosing; the piece is from a chess set.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Brooke was an English poet best known for his First World War sonnets, such as 'The Soldier'.

clue.text: Spooner’s swanky glove that’s found by stage

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a place, not a noun

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

blocks.note: swanky is posh and a glove is a mitt; swap their opening sounds, spelling the second word with one T

explanation.surface: A fancy glove is discovered near the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of the two words gives the answer; the double T of the glove is spelt as one, since only the sound matters.
explanation.definitionFit: The mosh pit is the area in front of the stage at a rock concert where fans dance wildly.

clue.text: Birds keep moving down south

indicators.note: in a down clue, moving the letter for this compass point down shifts it to the bottom, the end of the word

blocks.note: to keep is to save

explanation.surface: Flocks keep heading south for the winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South' names the letter that moves, which already sits at the front of the verb for keep; sliding it down to the bottom gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Aves is the scientific class name for all birds in zoological taxonomy.

clue.text: Struggles to contain constant sins

indicators.note: to contain something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to vie is to compete or struggle
c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light

explanation.surface: Someone battles to keep their persistent wrongdoings under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struggles' looks like a noun but is a verb, 'competes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vices are immoral habits or wrongdoings, close synonyms of sins.

clue.text: Catch duck missing from enclosure

indicators.note: something missing from a word has been taken out of it

blocks.note: in cricket a duck is a score of zero, shaped like the letter O
a coop is an enclosure for hens

explanation.surface: Grab the duck that has escaped from its pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the bird that got away, but it is a cricket score of nought, which becomes the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: To cop is British slang for catching or getting, as in 'cop a look' or 'cop it'.

clue.text: Counter back against family’s tirades

indicators.note: counter means opposite, so the letters run in the opposing direction

blocks.note: to back someone is to support or aid them
a tribe is a family group, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: Pushing back against a family's angry outbursts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter' looks like a verb or noun to define, but it is the signal to turn the next word round; 'against' just places the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter verbal attack, and a tirade is a long angry speech, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Overseers great in number having negative effects

blocks.note: super means great
taken as written
ten is a number
a dent is a setback, as in 'a dent in confidence'

explanation.surface: A large number of managers are doing more harm than good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great in number' reads as 'numerous', but each word is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Superintendents are officials who supervise or manage, the same role as overseers.
